At the height of the Trump trade war with China, when tariffs seemed to increase almost weekly, companies like Logitech responded by sharply raising prices on their products in the US.

Earlier this year, the US Supreme Court ruled those tariffs were illegal and must be refunded to the manufacturers. However, no company has yet been seen passing the refunds on to consumers, and a class-action lawsuit is now attempting to address this …

The Trump tariff saga

Last year, Trump seized on the US trade deficit with China and seemed to believe that hitting Chinese-made products with sweeping tariffs would force companies like Apple to bring manufacturing back to the US.

Of course, that was never going to happen. The US lacks the manufacturing infrastructure, expertise, and low-cost labour needed to make consumer electronics at the scale the major brands require.

Trump insisted throughout that the tariffs would be paid by China, but in reality they were paid by the US brands importing the finished goods, and the extra cost was passed on to consumers in the form of higher prices. At the height of the saga, the tariff rate reached as high as 145%.

Logitech, for example, raised prices on roughly half of its products by up to 25%.

Consumers deserve refunds

The US Supreme Court ultimately ruled that Trump had no authority to impose these tariffs unilaterally, and said the money already paid by US companies must be returned. That refund process is now under way.

The problem is that the costs were ultimately borne by consumers in the form of higher prices, yet none of the affected companies have signalled any plans to refund their customers.

Law firm CPM has filed a class-action lawsuit against Logitech, seeking refunds for consumers who paid the higher prices during the period the tariffs were in effect.

9to5Mac view

The principle is undeniable. The companies paid the tariff, passed the extra cost on to consumers, and now the government is refunding the money to the companies. Morally, they should refund that portion to customers who bought during the period.

In practice, though, it is extremely challenging. Logitech would need to identify all the relevant transactions across a large number of third-party retailers, track what each consumer paid, and work out what proportion of that was due to the tariff.

Even if the lawsuit ultimately succeeds, it could set a very interesting precedent — though it is worth noting that in class actions, the main beneficiaries are usually the lawyers, while the average payout to consumers tends to be small.
